Actually place ordinary paper gently and communicate in an approved tabletop setting, adapting to a response. Record action separately from future ideas and simulated school events.

pairs.material: Fiction: A quietly asks for paper in a reading corner and waits; B speaks clearly in an agreed class turn.
pairs.prompt: Who is making the reading-corner request?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who is speaking to the class?
pairs.explanation: Setting and communication needs differ; volume is not a moral ranking.

pairs.material: Original cards: A says “Reading corner: be considerate; ask for help if needed.” B says “Let the audience understand; assisted expression is welcome.”
pairs.prompt: Which fits this reading corner?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which fits a talk to an audience?
pairs.explanation: Use the setting and needs; quiet must not block help.

pairs.material: Story cards: A refers to natural bird and stream sounds; B uses feelings and considerate conduct as metaphors.
pairs.prompt: Which discusses natural sounds?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which uses metaphors?
pairs.explanation: A metaphor is not a body test; not hearing does not show disrespect.

pairs.material: Fiction: A made a reminder and displayed it with tabletop permission; B only plans to make one next time.
pairs.prompt: Who actually made and displayed it?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who has only a future plan?
pairs.explanation: Making, permission and display are separate; a plan is not action.

reflections: How did you consider the setting and someone’s needs? Record assistance, uncertainty and unfinished tasks without private medical information or a moral volume ranking.
What might you try next? Separate future ideas from consent and actions already taken.

lesson14.title: Everyone cares for shared property
lesson14.goal: Identify uses of shared facilities, read a complete observation record, observe and record safely, discuss care methods and act together with permission. Separate facts, uncertain causes and future suggestions.
lesson14.prerequisite: An adult may read. Use paper cards; actual care uses only a safe shared book or tabletop item approved by an adult. No electrical inspection is required.
lesson14.parentTip: Book facilities are not proof of your school’s facilities. Distinguish school, household-shared and personal objects. Observe only in an approved area; no fan testing, toilet operation, climbing or repair, chemicals or sharp fragments. Do not investigate classmates or collect names, photos or addresses. Ask responsible adults for help without confronting others or taking on repair. Observation, unknown cause and permission differ.

steps.title: Four campus objects and uses
steps.text: Page 52 shows a basketball court, electric fan, reading-room books and desks/chairs, each with a shared use. Shared access does not make an item someone’s personal possession. Household-shared items are not campus property.
steps.activity: Read all four and name each use. Compare original text cards for a school-library book and a personal pencil. Keep unknown school facilities unknown; do not operate the fan or court equipment.

steps.title: The full observation table: good, damaged, unknown
steps.text: Page 53 includes observer, time and place. The bucket is marked good, the table-tennis table damaged, and a third item/state row blank. Blank is neither good nor damaged, and visible condition does not establish a cause.
steps.activity: Read both filled rows and the blank. Make a separate card with nickname, date, general setting, object, visible condition and known/unknown cause. Actually observe one adult-approved safe campus object; a household-shared book may be used if labelled honestly. No permission means unfinished, not inspection of dangerous equipment.

steps.title: Two desks’ imagined wishes
steps.text: The two desks at the bottom of page 53 are marked and tidy respectively. Their personified wishes invite care; furniture does not literally speak, and a picture cannot identify who caused damage.
steps.activity: Read both personified examples and suggest each need. Offer an original response and listen to another suggestion. Do not pressure someone to comply or infer a person’s character from a desk.

steps.title: Discuss all four care methods
steps.text: Page 54 shows gentle use of a flush pedal, avoiding marks on walls, arranging cleaning tools and using a table mat. Care must suit the object; not every surface is washable and tools are not toys.
steps.activity: Read all four. Use fictional wall/tool cards to practice a considerate reminder, response and request for adult help. No toilet, long-tool or chemical operation. Actually use an approved shared book or tabletop item: follow agreed use, appropriate care and return; record each, not a paper-card simulation of repair.

steps.title: Act together, review and ask for help
steps.text: Correct use, routine care, reminders and reporting are different. Agreement is not execution. Avoid damaged or dangerous equipment and tell a trusted adult rather than dismantling it. Caring does not require taking risks.
steps.activity: Agree on a safe shared-tabletop action and roles, such as arranging two approved books. One places, one checks; swap roles. Review each contribution, facts and uncertainty. Separately role-play a fictional damage report; a reminder is not a completed repair. Future suggestions remain plans.

manual: Read all four court/fan/books/desks examples and name each use. Distinguish campus, household-shared and personal scope without inventing school facilities.
Read both filled bucket/table-tennis rows and the third blank row. Blank is unknown; condition alone does not prove a cause or identify a responsible person.

Actually observe an approved safe shared item and record nickname, date, general setting, object, visible state and known/unknown cause. Label a household substitute; do not invent school observations or inspect electrical/damaged equipment.
Read both desks’ personified wishes, name needs, offer an original response and hear a suggestion. Do not treat furniture as speaking or infer responsibility or character.
Discuss all four pedal/wall/tool/mat methods. Practice reminders and responses with paper cards; do not operate toilets, long tools or chemicals.
Actually use an approved shared book or tabletop item, recording agreed use, suitable care and return separately. No permission means unfinished; a paper card is not actual repair.
Actually agree on a shared-tabletop action and roles, contribute and swap checking, such as arranging two approved books. Label adult participation; do not claim a whole-class action.
Review a real care action, help and unknowns. Separately practice a fictional report to a trusted adult; do not repair or claim a reminder solved damage. Future ideas are separate.

pairs.material: Explicit cards: A is a school reading-room book available for classmates to borrow; B is the child’s personal pencil.
pairs.prompt: Which is campus shared property here?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which is personal here?
pairs.explanation: Scope is explicit, not changed by preference or who currently holds an item.

pairs.material: Book-table reading: A is the bucket marked good; B is the table-tennis table marked damaged. A third row is blank and causes unstated.
pairs.prompt: Which row is marked good?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which row is marked damaged?
pairs.explanation: Read the marks; blank is unknown, and the cause is not established.

pairs.material: Fiction: A observes a torn book page with unknown cause; B records adult permission to arrange books but has not acted.
pairs.prompt: Who records a visible condition?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only has permission, without action?
pairs.explanation: Observation, permission and action differ; do not fill unknown causes with guesses.

pairs.material: Fiction: A arranged approved shared books with agreement; B only plans to arrange them next time.
pairs.prompt: Who actually arranged books?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who has only a future plan?
pairs.explanation: Record real contribution separately from plans; not all objects are therefore repaired.

reflections: What did you actually observe or care for? State scope, help and unknown causes, without identifying classmates or treating personification as fact.
What might you do together next? Separate suggestions, permission, real contributions and future plans.

lesson15.title: We do not litter
lesson15.goal: Compare settings, read all six story panels, discuss shared hygiene and actually record or collect safe paper; distinguish observations, actions and plans.
lesson15.prerequisite: An adult can read the book; use only your own clean paper, a bag and a safe tabletop. No river visit, public waste handling or travel is required.
lesson15.parentTip: Do not touch unknown waste, sharp items, bodily fluids or cleaning chemicals, or enter water to retrieve litter. Tell a trusted adult about discomfort; never induce coughing or spitting. Masks require suitable adult and professional guidance. Follow local transport instructions and ask an adult about necessary food or water; textbook examples are not universal transport laws.

steps.title: Compare all four setting pictures
steps.text: Page 55 shows two pairs: spectator seating and a riverside, each with scattered waste and a tidier scene. Preferences can have personal reasons; pictures do not establish responsibility or local conditions.
steps.activity: Actually read or listen to all four pictures, describe visible items and compare each pair. Explain a preference without grading feelings. Mention a familiar tidy place only if actually observed; otherwise say unknown.

steps.title: No visible bin does not permit littering
steps.text: Page 56 includes a child with discomfort, a child holding a book and a child discarding paper because no bin is seen. Discomfort calls for care and adult help, rather than a character judgment.
steps.activity: Discuss all three roles. Use clean paper to rehearse keeping it in a bag and asking an adult where it belongs. Make a time, general place, observed action and suggestion record. Enter real observations only in an approved safe area; do not invent facts or photograph others.

steps.title: Three reminders and bodily needs
steps.text: Page 57 discusses covering coughs or sneezes, tissue disposal and masks during influenza. China CDC advises tissue or elbow coverage and suitable hand hygiene; mask use depends on actual circumstances, not a website diagnosis.
steps.activity: Read all three reminders and the open-ended continuation. Describe or model a disposal route with clean paper only; do not cough, spit or touch your mouth or nose. Ask an adult about discomfort; use an established safe washing method, never disinfectants.

steps.title: Four petals and real actions
steps.text: The four petals concern no spitting on the floor, no drawing on walls, taking waste when leaving and no eating on a metro or bus. These are textbook situations; follow local adult instructions and seek help for health needs.
steps.activity: Read all four petals and draw your own record. Colour only actions actually completed and explain the evidence; leave unknown or uncompleted actions blank and keep plans separate. This is not an automatic website award or a judgment of others.

steps.title: All six panels and safe paper collection
steps.text: The story across pages 55–57 progresses through bringing a bag, discarded picnic peel, paper play, waste left behind, collection and disposal at sorting bins. Having a bag does not prove collection or sorting.
steps.activity: Read or listen to all six panels and retell them in order. After agreement, place two pieces of your own clean paper on a safe table, collect them into a bag and restore the surface. Read local sorting guidance with an adult, not colours alone. A paper rehearsal is not an actual picnic or completed sorting; review facts and keep plans separate.

manual: Actually read all four seating and riverside pictures, describe visible differences and explain a preference without inventing local experience or responsibility.
Actually discuss all three page 56 roles and rehearse retaining clean paper and asking for help when no bin is visible; discomfort is not a moral fault.

Actually make a four-column time, general place, action and suggestion record; enter facts only after a real observation in an adult-approved safe area. Unknown or unapproved observations remain pending; collect no identities.

Actually read the three hygiene reminders and describe tissue or elbow coverage, suitable disposal and washing. Do not induce coughs, spit, handle fluids or disinfectants, or force an unsuitable mask.
Actually read all four petals and make a personal record; colour only completed actions, leave unknowns blank and separate future plans. Ask an adult about transport and bodily needs.
Actually read all six story panels in order and distinguish bringing a bag, collection and sorting; do not claim a personal picnic.

After agreement, actually place your own two clean paper pieces, collect them into a bag and restore a safe table; record the steps separately. Handle no unknown waste and conduct no riverside rehearsal.

Actually read the wording of local sorting guidance with an adult and say whether the paper destination is known. Missing guidance remains pending; colours are insufficient and collection is not sorting. Review real actions and plans.

pairs.material: Explicit fictional picture cards: A shows scattered paper on spectator seating; B shows tidy seating without scattered paper. Causes are unspecified.
pairs.prompt: Which card shows scattered paper?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which card shows no scattered paper?
pairs.explanation: Use visible facts; do not infer responsibility or grade preferences.

pairs.material: Fictional action cards: A retains clean waste paper in a bag but does not know its sorting destination; B has actually sorted suitable waste using local guidance supplied by an adult.
pairs.prompt: Who still lacks the sorting destination?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who has an actual guided sorting record?
pairs.explanation: Temporary retention is not completed sorting; do not guess from colours.

pairs.material: Fictional records: A describes paper actually seen on a table, with unknown cause; B only suggests preparing a bag next time.
pairs.prompt: Who records an actual observation?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who records a future suggestion?
pairs.explanation: An observation and a plan differ; unknown causes remain unknown.

pairs.material: Fictional steps: A has prepared a bag but paper remains on the table; B has collected paper and restored a safe table but has not sorted it.
pairs.prompt: Who has only prepared, without collection?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who has collected but not sorted?
pairs.explanation: Preparation, collection and sorting differ. Answers do not confirm real actions.

reflections: What did you actually observe or collect? Describe help and unknowns without identifying others.
How would you keep a place tidy next? Separate completed actions from future suggestions.

lesson16.title: Everyone queues in order
lesson16.goal: Compare distribution methods and learn order, spacing, arrival and numbered waiting. Read all six courtesy panels and actually rehearse tabletop turn-taking and communication; urgent needs allow adult help and plans remain separate.
lesson16.prerequisite: An adult can read the book. Use two personal paper cards and three role cards on a safe table; no staircase, station or crowd rehearsal is needed.
lesson16.parentTip: Do not create pushing, congestion, stair or boarding experiments or obstruct exits. Follow staff guidance in actual settings; tell an adult about discomfort or urgent needs rather than grading endurance or compulsory yielding. Courtesy begins with communication, not forced sacrifice. State adult participation; card ordering is not actual public queuing.

steps.title: Two distribution methods and turns
steps.text: Page 58 contrasts crowding around a box with receiving items in a queue. Preferences may have reasons and feelings are ungraded. Order helps participants know whose turn it is, without guaranteeing greater speed.
steps.activity: Read both pictures and describe visible methods. Agree how to use two of your own paper cards, each take and replace once, then reverse who goes first. Buy no gifts, take no other person’s belongings, do not push and do not claim a whole-class event.

steps.title: Why queue: two settings
steps.text: Page 59 contrasts crowding on stairs with orderly bus boarding. Order concerns safety and fairness, but does not replace hazard awareness, staff arrangements or help for urgent needs.
steps.activity: Read both pictures and discuss reasons. Make three role cards explicitly stating A arrived first, B next and C last, then arrange them accordingly. This is paper simulation only, not a stair or vehicle experiment; infer no actual injury.

steps.title: Three methods: spacing, arrival and calls
steps.text: Page 60 shows leaving space at a marked line, not inviting a friend to cut in, and sitting while waiting for a number. Queuing need not be a standing line; the pictured one-metre line is a local instruction, not a universal distance.
steps.activity: Read all three examples. Leave space between tabletop role cards, move one according to the agreed order, then let an adult call A, B and C and move only the called card. Arrival is explicitly given, not changed by friendship. Ask staff about different arrangements.

steps.title: All six courtesy panels
steps.text: The six bottom panels across pages 58–60 progress from later arrival and inviting an older person first, to asking about order and an adult offering a turn, then urgent toilet need and considering courtesy. Requests, offers, consent and actual yielding differ.
steps.activity: Read and retell all six in order. The ending is not a compulsory single answer for every situation; discuss communication. Use cards for toilet conversations only, never delay an actual bodily need or infer that everyone has identical needs.

steps.title: Three conversations, actual review and holiday plans
steps.text: Keeping turns, noticing needs and explaining your own difficulty can coexist. Ask an adult about special situations rather than forcibly changing a public queue. The book’s holiday reminder concerns future intentions.
steps.activity: Rehearse three safe tabletop conversations: joining behind, asking whether to yield, and explaining an urgent need while seeking adult help. Each includes a request and response before agreed card movement. A refusal can be explained with help; do not grade feelings. Review actual turns and conversations, then record future holiday or public-setting plans separately.

manual: Actually read both distribution pictures, describe crowding and ordered receipt and give a preference without grading feelings or promising greater speed.
Actually agree how to use your own two paper cards, each take and replace once and reverse the starting order. No pushing or invented class event; state adult involvement.
Actually read both stair and bus pictures and explain order, safety and fairness. Arrange three role cards by their explicitly stated arrival; no real staircase or vehicle experiments.
Actually read all three spacing, arrival/no-cutting and seated-number examples. The pictured one-metre line is local, not a universal distance.
Actually space tabletop role cards, move them by agreed turns and then by an adult’s call. Friendship does not alter arrival; do not claim a public event.
Actually read all six courtesy panels in order and distinguish requests, offers, consent and yielding. An open ending is not a compulsory universal answer.
Actually rehearse joining behind, asking about courtesy and explaining urgent needs to an adult, with request and response before agreed movement. Do not force yielding or delay bodily needs.
Actually review completed turns, communication and help; record holiday or public-setting plans separately. Correct web answers do not confirm actions.

pairs.material: Explicit fictional record: A arrived at a service point first; B arrived after A. Staff specify arrival order with no other arrangement.
pairs.prompt: Who goes first under this rule?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who goes later under this rule?
pairs.explanation: Use the stated order; ask staff about special arrangements.

pairs.material: Explicit method cards: A sits in a waiting area for a staff number call; B stands in an ordered line. Both follow the agreed method.
pairs.prompt: Which is seated numbered waiting?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which is standing in line?
pairs.explanation: Queuing can take different forms, following the setting’s arrangement.

pairs.material: Fictional courtesy records: A has only asked whether the other person needs an earlier turn and received no response; B yielded after mutual agreement.
pairs.prompt: Who has only asked, without consent?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who actually yielded after consent?
pairs.explanation: Request, agreement and action differ; courtesy is not forced.

pairs.material: Fictional records: A actually completed agreed safe tabletop turns today; B only plans to follow local queues during a holiday.
pairs.prompt: Who records an action already done?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who records a future plan?
pairs.explanation: Tabletop rehearsal is not an actual public event, and plans are not completed actions.

reflections: How did you actually take turns or communicate? Describe help, responses and unknown local rules.
How would you queue or explain needs next? Separate plans from completed actions.

lower.title: Ethics and the Rule of Law · Grade 1 Lower
lower.goal: Reflect on actual experience, distinguish goals from action, and break a suitable small goal into steps to try.

steps.title: Reflecting on experience
steps.text: Page 2 reflects on earlier goals. Describe an actual attempt, something not yet achieved, or choose not to share. Learners need not have the same experiences.
steps.activity: Discuss an actual experience you are comfortable sharing.

steps.title: Goals and action
steps.text: Page 3 discusses direction and persistence. Original scenario: He wants a tidy desk and has put two pencils into the case today. The intention and completed action are different.
steps.activity: Describe a small goal separately from an actual attempt.

steps.title: Personal and shared goals
steps.text: Page 4 separates personal and class goals. Choose a suitable personal goal; shared goals require real discussion. A web submission is not agreement by classmates.
steps.activity: Discuss a possible shared family goal with the adult, or leave this pending.

steps.title: Small steps and adjustment
steps.text: Page 5 discusses small steps, planning and persistence. Original example: tidy a desk by putting pencils away, then books. Choose safe, suitable steps. Sporting examples are not universal targets.
steps.activity: Break a chosen goal into two steps and actually try the first.

steps.title: Recording an attempt
steps.text: Record actual steps and where help is needed, then separately note future plans. An unfinished goal can still involve progress; no character score is assigned.
steps.activity: Record attempts separately from plans in your own words.

pairs.material: Original scenario: He wants a tidy desk and puts two pencils back in the case today.
pairs.prompt: What is the goal in this scenario?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which action happened today?
pairs.explanation: Read the goal separately from the completed action.

pairs.material: Original two-step plan: put pencils away, then books. Only the first step was tried today.
pairs.prompt: What comes first in the plan?
pairs.reviewPrompt: What comes next in the plan?
pairs.explanation: The sequence is explicit; an untried second step is not completed.

pairs.material: Original record: An suggests a shared goal but has not discussed it with anyone else.
pairs.prompt: Which event has happened?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which event has not happened?
pairs.explanation: A suggestion is not completed discussion or real agreement.

manual: Actually discuss a past attempt or unfinished goal you are comfortable sharing.
Actually choose a suitable small goal and explain why you want to try it.
Actually discuss a shared goal with the adult; without discussion, do not confirm agreement.
Actually split your goal into two steps and try the first; record the result and ask for help when needed.
reflections: Record an actual step, feeling or area where help is needed.
Separately record what you plan to try or adjust next; do not mark it as achieved.

lesson2.title: Doing things carefully
lesson2.goal: Explore the cause and effects of an omission, try checklists and reminders, and compare systematically without missing positions.
lesson2.prerequisite: Have printed pages 6–9 of the lower volume, paper, a pencil and existing supplies ready. An adult may read aloud. Keep the textbook comparison pending if unavailable; record an original paper alternative separately.
lesson2.parentTip: One mistake does not define a child as careless. Do not require personal disclosure or judge classmates’ character. Explore causes and try methods; drawings can serve as reminders. View the textbook pictures on the original page; draw our separate six-position activity on paper. A choice answer does not replace comparison.

steps.title: Observing an omission
steps.text: Page 6 shows mistakes with buttons, missing belongings or questions, and a forgotten book; pages 6–7 continue the book-and-help story. Share an experience only if you want to, or discuss a fictional card. One omission does not define a person.
steps.activity: Actually examine the page or original card with the adult and describe an omission and its effects.

steps.title: Exploring causes without blame
steps.text: Page 7 discusses misreading, rushing and forgetting to check. Original scenario: Xiao He reads only the first line and misses a question on the second; Xiao An notices it while checking. Use the stated cause without labeling real classmates.
steps.activity: Actually discuss a method that could be adjusted; different reasonable approaches are valid.

steps.title: Checklists and reminders
steps.text: Page 8 presents notes, checklists and mutual reminders. Draw three existing supplies, check one at a time and mark each checked item. Name the specific task and thank a helper without teasing. Choose a useful list based on actual needs, not the longest list.
steps.activity: Actually make and use a small checklist, then exchange a specific reminder with the adult.

steps.title: Comparing position by position
steps.text: Page 9 compares two pictures using systematic scanning and marks. View those pictures in the textbook. Original paper alternative: draw A with ○△□ on both rows; draw B with ○□□ on the top row and △△○ on the bottom. Number positions 1–6, top row first, left to right. Differences are at 2, 4 and 6; these are not answers to the textbook pictures.
steps.activity: Actually compare the textbook pictures, or separately draw and compare the original pair, marking and checking every position. State which activity was used.

steps.title: Checking before recording
steps.text: Describe the method actually used and where help was needed. Careful comparison is not a speed race. Leave unfinished work pending; planning to use a list is not having checked it.
steps.activity: Record actual methods separately from plans.

pairs.material: Original scenario: Xiao He reads only the first line and misses the second-line question; Xiao An discovers it while checking.
pairs.prompt: What does Xiao He do before the omission?
pairs.reviewPrompt: What does Xiao An do when noticing it?
pairs.explanation: Distinguish the stated actions without judging a real child’s character.

pairs.material: Original checklist: pencil, eraser and book. The pencil and book have been checked; the eraser has not.
pairs.prompt: Which item has not been checked?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which of these two items has been checked?
pairs.explanation: Unchecked does not mean missing; record actual checking for each item.

pairs.material: Original two-row diagrams: A has ○△□ on both rows. B has ○□□ on the top and △△○ below. Top positions are 1–3 and bottom positions 4–6.
pairs.prompt: What is at position 2 in diagram A?
pairs.reviewPrompt: What is at position 2 in diagram A in this new pair?
pairs.explanation: Read the current diagram at the specified position. A’s second position is a triangle in the original pair and a square in the new review pair. View the textbook pictures separately.
pairs.reviewMaterial: New original review diagrams, different from the earlier pair: A has ○□□ on the top and ○△□ below. B has ○△□ on the top and △△○ below. Top positions are 1–3 and bottom positions 4–6.

pairs.material: Original checking record: positions 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 have been compared; position 5 has not.
pairs.prompt: Which position has not been compared?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which of these two positions has been compared?
pairs.explanation: Check coverage of positions; a checked position need not contain a difference.

manual: Actually discuss an omission’s effects and possible causes using the page or an original card; personal disclosure is optional.
Actually make a three-item picture or word checklist and check existing objects one at a time; do not mark an unchecked item as checked.
Actually exchange a specific reminder and response with the adult; thank a helper without teasing.
Actually complete page 9’s comparison, or separately draw and check the original six-position pair. State which material was used rather than claiming the textbook activity was done.
reflections: Record a discovery from actual checking, reminders or comparison and any help needed.
Separately record a checking method you plan to try; do not mark it as already used.

lesson3.title: Putting mistakes right
lesson3.goal: Distinguish acknowledging an action, apologizing and making amends; try finding a cause, asking for a reminder and a new method, and record actual attempts and feelings.
lesson3.prerequisite: Describe an event with adult help. Use our original story or a voluntary everyday slip; private experiences need not be disclosed. A learning difficulty is not automatically a moral fault.
lesson3.parentTip: Avoid humiliation, forced confession or public disclosure. Ask a trusted adult to handle harm or danger first. Agree on appropriate repairs under real rules; children must not handle unknown dirty or dangerous objects. An apology does not require immediate forgiveness. Keep role-play, one attempt, lasting habits and future plans separate.

steps.title: Describe the facts honestly
steps.text: The textbook starts with accidentally dirtying a borrowed book and introduces acknowledgment and apology. Establish what happened and your own part rather than taking responsibility for everyone else. In our rehearsal, He marked a peer’s scrap paper and is willing to explain and discuss a repair.
steps.activity: Use our scrap-paper story or a voluntary everyday example to actually say what happened, what you did and its effect. Names and private details are unnecessary.

steps.title: An apology and a repair are separate actions
steps.text: After expressing regret, ask what could help. Saying sorry does not mean damage has been repaired or require immediate forgiveness. Our paper scenario involves agreeing to provide another sheet. For real borrowed items, follow the librarian’s or teacher’s instructions rather than washing or paying for them independently.
steps.activity: Actually rehearse an explanation, apology and listening with an adult, then rehearse one agreed paper repair. A rehearsal is not proof a real incident has been resolved.

steps.title: Find a cause and ask for a reminder
steps.text: The textbook discusses timely correction, causes and asking for reminders. Our story names a specific cause: rushing to tidy up without looking at the table. One method is to slow down and look before taking paper. Ask a trusted adult for a specific reminder. Calling a child bad is not a cause or a method.
steps.activity: Discuss one concrete cause of an actual slip or our story, agree on a method and request a helpful reminder. Making a plan is not trying it.

steps.title: Try a different method for real
steps.text: The textbook considers habits, lessons, difficulties and new methods discovered through correction. Repeated learning confusion can also need a teacher’s help; not every difficulty is deliberate wrongdoing. Our rehearsal method is to look at the table, put pens away, then take clean paper. Try it once and examine the result.
steps.activity: Actually try a safe, ordinary method with an adult and describe the result. Label a story rehearsal; one attempt does not establish a lasting habit.

steps.title: Notice real changes and express your feelings
steps.text: Listening to reminders, trying methods and asking for help can improve a situation gradually. A mistake does not define the whole person. Several attempts may be needed, and an unsuccessful attempt can be recorded honestly. Keep actual repairs separate from future intentions; apologies are not counted as morality points.
steps.activity: Review what really happened and what help is still needed. Write next week’s intentions separately; do not turn a plan into a completed habit.

pairs.material: Our story: He explained marking the scrap paper and expressed regret but has not repaired it. Lin agreed with the peer and supplied another sheet but has not yet explained their own action. We compare actions, not the whole person.
pairs.prompt: Who has explained their own action and expressed regret?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who has performed the agreed repair?
pairs.explanation: An apology and an actual repair are separate. Each person has done only one stated action; neither action counts as both.

pairs.material: Ning wrote a plan to put pens away before taking paper but has not tried it. An actually organized the pens, took a sheet using the method and recorded the result.
pairs.prompt: Who has actually tried the method?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who currently has only a plan?
pairs.explanation: An actual attempt may be recorded as done; a written plan remains pending. One attempt is not proof of a lasting habit.

pairs.material: The record says rushing to tidy without looking at the table was this incident’s cause. Looking at the table before taking paper is the agreed method for next time.
pairs.prompt: Which statement describes the specific cause this time?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which statement describes the method for next time?
pairs.first: Rushing to tidy without looking at the table
pairs.second: Looking at the table before taking paper
pairs.explanation: A cause explains the event; a method describes what to do later. Proposing it does not mean it was tried.

pairs.material: Zhu actually asked an adult to remind them to look before taking paper. He intends to make that request tomorrow but has not said it yet.
pairs.prompt: Who has already requested a reminder?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Whose request is still a future intention?
pairs.explanation: Check whether the request happened. An intention is not a completed action. Asking for help does not make a child bad or prove everything is fixed.

manual: Using our story or a voluntary everyday event, actually explain what happened, your action and its effect, then rehearse an apology. Label simulation and never require private disclosures.
Actually listen to an adult playing the other person and rehearse an agreed paper repair. Follow adult rules in real situations; no dangerous materials or forced immediate forgiveness.
Actually discuss one cause, agree on a method and ask a trusted adult for a specific reminder. Record discussion or the request without claiming the method was tried.
Actually try one safe method with an adult and examine the result. Record a real attempt or a rehearsal; one success does not establish a long-term habit.
reflections: Describe the explanation, repair or method attempt that really happened, your feelings and any help needed. An unfinished action may be recorded honestly; feelings are not graded.
What will you try next time? Keep future plans separate; untried methods and continuing practice do not mean everything is already fixed.

lesson4.title: Participating with energy
lesson4.goal: Explore participation, rest, suitable activity and feelings; try attentive reading, understandable expression and enjoyable singing using accessible ways.
lesson4.prerequisite: Speech, pointing, assistive communication and adult transcription are welcome. Caregivers supply familiar, lawful reading and song material. No uniform voice or posture is required.
lesson4.parentTip: Do not judge character by appearance, body shape, volume, disability, tiredness or feelings. Do not insist on continuing when unwell; tell a trusted adult what is needed. Reading, expression and singing may happen separately and use assistive methods. No costumes, contest entry, recordings or photos are required.

steps.title: Energy is more than appearance
steps.text: The textbook’s procession and animal story invite discussion beyond looks, including voice, posture and enthusiasm. We do not turn those into pupil rankings: attractive clothes do not prove attentive participation, and a quiet voice does not mean no effort.
steps.activity: Actually view printed pages 14–16 or listen to an adult and discuss why appearance and actions are different. Do not compare classmates’ looks.

steps.title: Talk about rest, movement and feelings
steps.text: The textbook connects suitable activity, rest and feelings. Today’s state differs between people. Being tired, sad or uncomfortable can be discussed with an adult; smiling constantly is not required. Choose suitable movement with adult guidance. One attempt does not establish long-term health.
steps.activity: Actually review rest, suitable activity or feelings with an adult and identify one need and helpful response. Keep a future change as a separate plan.

steps.title: Try attentive reading
steps.text: The textbook includes attentive reading. Use a familiar short line or lawful adult-provided material at a comfortable pace. Adult-led reading, pointing and assistive communication are possible. This is not a competition for loudness or perfect first attempts.
steps.activity: Actually read, follow an adult or express a familiar passage accessibly. Record the method and help used; an unattempted activity stays pending.

steps.title: Make your meaning understandable
steps.text: The textbook includes clear spoken expression. Our focus is understanding: face the listener, express one idea, allow pauses and ask for help without shouting. Picture cards and assistive tools may be used. Have the listener repeat the meaning and check it.
steps.activity: Actually express one idea to an adult and check their understanding. Record speech, pictures or another assistive method without grading volume.

steps.title: Join a song and review each activity
steps.text: The textbook also includes enjoyable singing. Sing part of a familiar lawful song, follow its rhythm or participate accessibly; a happy facial expression is not compulsory. Reading, expression and singing are separate tasks, not three completions for doing one.
steps.activity: Actually join a short song or rhythm activity and review each of the three attempts with an adult. Pause when tired and keep next steps as plans; no automatic ranking of energy.

pairs.material: Record: Ning selected attractive clothes but has not started reading. Zhu attentively read a familiar short line at a comfortable pace.
pairs.prompt: Who has an actual reading record?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who has only prepared their appearance, with reading still pending?
pairs.explanation: Appearance preparation and actual reading differ. Clothes and looks do not earn character or energy scores.

pairs.material: Record: He actually told an adult they feel tired and need rest. An intends to say this later but has not expressed it yet.
pairs.prompt: Who has already told an adult about the current need?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only plans to express it later?
pairs.explanation: An actual expression differs from a plan. Tiredness is not a character fault; asking for help may be recorded honestly.

pairs.material: Activity card: the first task is attentive reading of familiar short lines; the second is expressing an idea to a listener and checking understanding. Both may use suitable assistive methods.
pairs.prompt: Which task is this reading activity?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which task is this spoken or assistive expression activity?
pairs.explanation: Reading and expression are different tasks. Doing one does not complete the other; assistive participation is not lesser participation.

pairs.material: Record: Ning actually joined part of a familiar song through its rhythm. Zhu only wrote a plan to join next time and has not tried yet.
pairs.prompt: Who has an actual song or rhythm participation record?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who currently only has a future plan?
pairs.explanation: Record the real method used. A plan is not participation; no standard voice, posture or happy expression is required.

manual: Actually view printed pages 14–16 or listen to an adult, discuss appearance versus participation and review a need involving rest, movement or feelings and possible help. Do not grade looks or feelings.
Actually read, follow along or express a familiar lawful passage accessibly. Record method, attempted content and help; do not confirm reading that never happened.
Actually express an idea to an adult and check their repeated understanding. Label speech, pointing, assistive communication or transcription honestly without shouting or private disclosure.
Actually sing, follow rhythm or join part of a familiar lawful song accessibly. Record what happened; pause when tired without forced smiles or performance.
reflections: Describe each reading, expression or song attempt that happened, your feelings and needed help. Unfinished tasks may be recorded honestly; feelings and volume are not graded.
What would you like to try next, when might you rest or ask for help? Keep plans separate; one participation does not prove permanent ideal condition.

lesson5.title: Being together
lesson5.goal: Share a story of doing things together, rehearse joining requests and responses, agree on rules and take turns, and practise comfort, fair yielding and understanding.
lesson5.prerequisite: Use paper slips or a familiar safe activity with a caregiver; existing peers are not required. Speech, pictures, assistive communication and adult transcription are welcome and labelled honestly.
lesson5.parentTip: Participation needs willingness on both sides. A polite request does not guarantee entry, and refusal is not a character judgment. Pause, change activities or ask an adult for help. Do not force toy sharing, yielding all opportunities or immediate forgiveness. Use safe tabletop activities rather than chasing or collisions.

steps.title: Tell a story of being together
steps.text: The textbook begins with stories of playing and sharing reading. Tell a real experience or clearly discuss a book example; a book story is not your own experience. Happiness and having many friends are not required.
steps.activity: Actually tell or draw a real story with activity and feelings, or label a textbook discussion. Do not disclose others’ identities.

steps.title: Ask politely before joining
steps.text: The book offers greetings, polite requests, bringing materials to discuss joining and asking for an introduction. A request opens discussion; having a toy does not require acceptance, and polite words are not actual participation. Listen to yes, later or no and discuss a workable response.
steps.activity: Actually rehearse all four approaches with an adult, each with a request and response. Use existing paper materials without buying toys or claiming peers agreed.

steps.title: Agree on rules and take turns
steps.text: The textbook explores game rules and how to continue after wins or losses. Our original tabletop activity: two people take turns putting their paper slips in their own small circles, one per turn, two turns each, with no contest or collisions. Both agree before starting. Pause to discuss disagreements rather than changing rules independently.
steps.activity: Actually agree on this rule with a willing adult and take two turns each. If agreement has not happened, record rules as pending rather than completed cooperation.

steps.title: Try comfort, fair yielding and understanding separately
steps.text: The textbook presents these three approaches. Our rehearsals: ask an upset person whether company is wanted; agree who goes first while preserving both people’s turns; listen to an explanation after slips are accidentally disturbed and agree on restoring them. Understanding does not force instant forgiveness or silence about discomfort.
steps.activity: Actually rehearse all three situations with an adult and listen to each response. Keep both people’s opportunities; express feelings and pause for help when needed.

steps.title: Review the process and your feelings
steps.text: Requesting, receiving a response, agreeing rules, participating and handling disagreement are different steps. A declined request can still show actual expression and a need for help. Friend count, winning and emotions do not earn character scores. One activity does not establish friendship; plans stay separate.
steps.activity: Review the story, four requests, actual rule-based activity and three friendly approaches. Label simulation or real activity without inventing events.

pairs.material: Record: Ning politely requested to join and still awaits an answer. Zhu heard agreement and began participating under the shared rules.
pairs.prompt: Who received agreement and started participating?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who is still waiting for a response?
pairs.explanation: Request, response and participation differ. Politeness does not mean agreement; waiting is not a fault.

pairs.material: Our rule cards: A says one paper slip per turn. B says alternate turns with two turns for each person. Both rules need agreement before use.
pairs.prompt: Which card states how many slips per turn?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which card states order and both people’s opportunities?
pairs.explanation: Quantity and turn-taking are separate. A written rule is not evidence both people agreed.

pairs.material: He asked an upset partner if company was wanted and received agreement to sit together. An agreed the partner goes first for one turn while retaining the next turn.
pairs.prompt: Who offered comfort with a response?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who fairly yielded a first turn while keeping both opportunities?
pairs.explanation: Comfort and fair turns differ. Neither means surrendering all opportunities or forcing immediate happiness.

pairs.material: Ning and an adult agreed on the paper rules and actually completed alternating turns. Zhu only wrote a plan for next time without asking or participating.
pairs.prompt: Who has a record of this actual shared activity?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who currently has only a future plan?
pairs.explanation: Completion differs from intention. Label adult participation or rehearsal rather than claiming classmates joined.

manual: Actually tell or draw a story and express feelings. Separate real experience from textbook discussion; discussion is valid without a prior experience or private names.
Actually rehearse greeting, polite requesting, discussing existing materials and asking for an introduction, with a response each time. Pause after refusal and do not claim peers agreed.

With a willing adult, actually agree on the original paper rule and alternate two turns each with one slip per turn. Record the real two-person activity and partner category; discussing rules alone is not participation.
Actually rehearse all three: comfort and a response, fair first-turn yielding, and listening and agreeing on restoring disturbed slips. Label simulation without forced forgiveness or happiness.
reflections: Describe an actual request, shared activity or disagreement and your feelings. Unsuccessful attempts and needed help may be recorded without grading friends or wins.
What invitation or method would you try next? Keep plans separate without inventing agreement or participation.

lesson6.title: Please help me
lesson6.goal: Recognize different difficulties and safe attempts versus adult help; rehearse explaining needs to suitable people, responses, gratitude and passing on safe help.
lesson6.prerequisite: Use paper difficulties and adult role-play without real losses, hazards or calls. Ask a trusted adult if you are unsure whether an attempt is safe.
lesson6.parentTip: Do not visit water, climb trees or approach smoke, fire or unexplained loud sounds to practise. Discuss hazards on paper and let trusted adults or responsible personnel handle them. Do not identify strangers by clothes or leave with them. Asking for help is not a character fault; seek another suitable adult after no response. Ask before helping and stay within your ability.

steps.title: Everyone can encounter difficulties
steps.text: The textbook gives examples involving pens, laces, unfamiliar words and items in water. A learning difficulty and a dangerous scene differ; concerns can be expressed honestly. Our cards describe needs without creating real problems.
steps.activity: Actually describe a voluntary ordinary difficulty or read a fictional card and state the event and need without private details.

steps.title: Check safety before attempting
steps.text: Printed page 23 considers lost belongings, unfamiliar rope skills, getting lost, an item in a tree, smoke and a distant loud sound. A safe manageable task may be tried first and help requested if needed. Getting lost, high or water locations, smoke and unexplained sounds need a trusted adult; do not climb, enter water or approach to investigate. Not every child can independently do the same task.
steps.activity: Actually discuss all six textbook scenarios, then classify our explicit tabletop paper task and hazard cards and explain why. No real-site experiments; correct classification does not handle a hazard.

steps.title: Choose suitable help and explain the need
steps.text: The book includes a kite in a tree and requesting caregiver contact after collection has not arrived. Our explicit roles assign reading guidance to a teacher and pickup checks to designated school staff. Clothing alone does not establish trust; do not leave alone with unknown people.
steps.activity: Actually rehearse the event, need and suitable helper with an adult and hear a response. Contact is role-play without calls or leaving school independently.

steps.title: Responses, thanks and resolution differ
steps.text: Agreement to help does not mean a difficulty is solved; responsible adults still check follow-up. Thanks can be spoken or expressed with pictures. With no response, do not blame yourself or invent help; seek another suitable trusted adult.
steps.activity: Actually rehearse thanks after agreement and a further request when help is temporarily unavailable. Label rehearsal rather than a resolved real problem.

steps.title: Pass on safe help
steps.text: Printed page 25 shows receiving help, gratitude and later helping someone else. Our paper exercise: ask whether an adult needs a slip and pass it after agreement. Receiving and giving are different actions. Helping does not justify approaching danger or doing tasks beyond your ability.
steps.activity: Actually receive safe paper help and thank it, then ask and pass a paper slip with agreement. Review the five activities; future help stays a plan.

pairs.material: Original cards: A is seated tabletop paper within easy reach under adult-confirmed safe arrangements; B is an item in water, discussed only on paper, requiring a trusted adult without the child entering water.
pairs.prompt: Which card is this safe ordinary tabletop attempt?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which card needs adult handling without entering water?
pairs.explanation: Use explicit safety conditions; calling something small does not prove every child can do it. The hazard card is discussion only.

pairs.material: Explicit fictional roles: Zhou guides reading; Lin is designated school pickup-contact staff who checks changes. Actual school roles need separate confirmation.
pairs.prompt: Who should hear about a reading difficulty in these cards?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who should check a pickup change in these cards?
pairs.explanation: Use stated responsibilities, not clothes. Schools and caregivers confirm real arrangements.

pairs.material: Ning explained a need in adult role-play and heard agreement, but the paper difficulty has not been handled. An only planned a future request without saying it.
pairs.prompt: Who has a request-and-response rehearsal record?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only has a future request plan?
pairs.explanation: A response is not resolution; a plan is not an actual request. Do not invent events.

pairs.material: Paper record: He received a slip from an adult and expressed thanks. Zhu asked whether help was wanted, received agreement and passed a slip to the adult.
pairs.prompt: Who received help and thanked it?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who gave help after agreement?
pairs.explanation: Receiving, thanking and giving are distinct real actions. One does not complete the other or handle a real hazard.

manual: Actually describe an ordinary difficulty and need or read our card. Private experiences need not be disclosed; create no loss or hazard.

Actually discuss all six scenarios on printed page 23, then classify our explicit tabletop and hazard cards with reasons. No climbing, water or smoke experiments; source discussion stays pending without complete material.
Actually rehearse choosing a helper by stated role, explaining a need and hearing the response. Pickup contact is role-play without calls or leaving with strangers.
Actually rehearse both thanks after agreement and seeking another suitable adult when help is unavailable. Do not claim the issue was solved.
Actually receive safe paper help and thank it, then ask and give paper help after agreement. Record the two actions separately without claiming real hazards or future plans are handled.
reflections: Describe an actual judgment or request rehearsal, its response and remaining needs. Worry and unresolved difficulties may be recorded without character scores.
Whose help might you need or how could you safely help next? Keep plans separate from agreement, rehearsal or real resolution.

lesson7.title: We enjoy sharing
lesson7.goal: Experience sharing books, methods and game rules; practise care, return, conditions and special-item boundaries while respecting both people’s choices.
lesson7.prerequisite: Choose ordinary safe materials you freely wish to share. An adult may read; stories, books and music must come from existing lawful material.
lesson7.parentTip: Sharing is voluntary. Do not demand private possessions, reciprocal promises or immediate forgiveness. A cherished keepsake may remain unloaned. For damage, explain honestly, stop using it and ask an adult to discuss suitable repair; apology does not mean repaired. Food examples are discussion only, not a tasting or sharing task. Keep private information private; worrying or harmful secrets may be told to a trusted adult.

steps.title: From one book to a shared story
steps.text: Page 26 shows personal reading, reading together, telling and acting a story. These are four different stages. Sharing content and enjoyment does not guarantee everyone immediately feels happy.
steps.activity: With one existing lawful suitable short story, actually read or hear it, agree to read together, tell it to the other person and agree on roles for a short seated or accessible scene without dangerous actions.

steps.title: Share a method and a game rule
steps.text: Page 27 gives construction, food and game examples. Explain a method and give the listener a chance to try. The site substitutes tabletop paper for jumping; food is discussed without handling or tasting.
steps.activity: With agreement, demonstrate and explain folding a paper card; let the other person try their own. Then explain taking turns pointing first to one’s own card and then to the other’s. Each person tries one round and exchanges an opportunity to explain.

steps.title: Share together and care for belongings
steps.text: Page 28 includes method guidance, book care, story expression and courtesy. Different content needs a suitable approach and a listener’s response. Private information need not be public; worrying or harmful secrets can be discussed with a trusted adult.
steps.activity: Ask to share an ordinary book or card, agree to view it at the table and when to return it, hear consent, handle it gently, view together, return and thank. Use a non-private original story for one line of telling and one response.

steps.title: Distinguish accidents, conditions and exceptions
steps.text: Page 29 discusses accidental damage, sharing requests and a treasured keepsake. A request is not consent. Conditions may be discussed and a loan declined. Apology, repair and forgiveness are distinct; never damage real belongings to practise.
steps.activity: Rehearse three fictional cards separately: report a torn paper card, stop using it and seek adult repair discussion; request table-only viewing and hear a response; explain that a keepsake is not loaned and offer a photo or oral description instead.

steps.title: Record actual sharing and personal feelings
steps.text: Pages 28–29 discuss enjoyment and ways of getting along. Someone may share a method while keeping a particular object private. Feelings vary. Label adult role-play separately from sharing with real classmates.
steps.activity: Look back at the four book stages, method, game, item and three communication rehearsals. Actually express one attempt and one response, orally or accessibly. Leave undone items pending and record future sharing separately.

manual: With a lawful familiar short story, actually read or hear it, agree to read together, tell it and agree on roles for a short scene. Record each of the four stages; leave missing stages pending and label adult role-play.
Actually demonstrate and explain folding a card, give the other person a chance to try and hear a response. Saying that a method exists is not sharing it.
Actually explain the tabletop paper game, let both people try a round and exchange an explaining opportunity. Website answers or discussion of the textbook jumping game are not actual play.
With actual consent, share an ordinary book or card, follow agreed care and return, thank, then tell and respond to a non-private story. Do not take anything without consent.

Actually rehearse all three fictional communications: honest accident reporting and adult repair discussion; a table-use condition and response; a special keepsake refusal with another sharing option. No real damage or forced forgiveness.

Actually review the separate records and express one real attempt and response, including unfinished items. Record next-time plans separately; discussion, role-play and feelings are not real-classmate events.

pairs.material: Fictional records: He reads a story and, with agreement, actually reads together, tells it and performs a short scene with an adult. Zhu only plans future shared reading.
pairs.prompt: Who has all four actual book-sharing stages recorded?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only has a future plan here?
pairs.explanation: Personal reading, shared reading, telling and acting each need an actual action. Adult role-play is not a classmate event.

pairs.material: Fictional materials: A is an ordinary card its owner is willing to view together at the table. B is a treasured keepsake the owner explicitly will not loan.
pairs.prompt: Which item may be viewed together with mutual consent?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which owner’s non-loan boundary should be respected?
pairs.explanation: Voluntary sharing and boundaries coexist. Declining a loan does not make a child unfriendly.

pairs.material: Fictional communication: Ning notices a shared card is torn, reports it, stops using it and asks an adult to discuss repair. An asks for table-only viewing before use and hears consent.
pairs.prompt: Which record discusses repair after an accident?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which record agrees on a condition before sharing?
pairs.explanation: Accident communication and prior conditions differ; apology or consent does not establish repair or an actual activity.

pairs.material: Fictional actions: He demonstrates a paper fold and lets the other person try. Zhu explains the tabletop card rule and both try a round.
pairs.prompt: Which record shares a making method?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which record shares a game rule with actual trials?
pairs.explanation: Methods and game rules each involve explanation, response and trying. These paper activities do not establish food sharing or physical exercise.

reflections: What did you actually share or hear, and how did the other person respond? You may name what you wish to share and what remains private. No forced disclosure or grading of feelings.
How might you explain a method, care for belongings or state a condition next time? Plans stay separate; hoped-for acceptance or forgiveness is not an event already achieved.

lesson8.title: Let us cooperate
lesson8.goal: Observe solo and cooperative processes; actually divide work, coordinate, exchange opportunities and discuss role disagreements; read the full story and distinguish safe simulation.
lesson8.prerequisite: An adult may read the source and familiar lawful material. Two willing participants use ordinary tabletop cards without blindfolds or carrying people.
lesson8.parentTip: Textbook blindfold, skipping, river and climbing scenes are discussion sources. The site does not reproduce those actions. Cooperation does not guarantee speed, happiness or success every time; inspect this actual process. Roles require agreement and may change or pause without coercion. Label adult participation separately from real classroom events and plans.

steps.title: What changes when there is cooperation?
steps.text: Page 30 contrasts a nose-placement activity without and with a helper’s prompts. Discuss visible differences without claiming every collaboration is faster or solo work is bad. Our visible tabletop target is an original communication substitute, not blindfolded movement.
steps.activity: Draw a circle and square on paper. First the child sees a specified target and places a paper piece independently. Then agree that an adult names the square; the child listens, confirms and places it. Compare how each target was known, without speed or moral scoring.

steps.title: Divide work and contribute
steps.text: Page 31 shows shared cleaning, play and recitation. The site tidies ordinary tabletop paper, not actual school cleaning or sports. Each person must do the agreed contribution rather than one person doing everything.
steps.activity: Agree a shared goal: divide six cards into two groups of three. One sorts and one checks; both actually do their part. Exchange roles and repeat. Separately play a tabletop pointing game for two turns each, without real rubbish or cleaning products.

steps.title: Learn together and record this effect
steps.text: Page 31 also shows joint recitation. Familiar lawful short material can be read or spoken in turns with prompts. Accuracy or greater ease needs actual observation; standing together does not prove efficiency. Accessible expression can be coordinated.
steps.activity: Choose two familiar lawful lines. Both first try reading or listening and speaking, agree turns and prompts, then jointly read or speak once and each check a line. Record specific help without racing, forced memorisation or declaring it faster.

steps.title: Discuss role disagreements before deciding
steps.text: Page 32 has four scenes involving the same desired role, refusing another role, withdrawing and blame. Read all four before discussing. State and hear wishes, discuss rotation, other roles or a pause. Declining a role is not lack of solidarity.
steps.activity: With original card-introducer and card-pointer roles, separately rehearse responses to both wanting to introduce, not wanting to point, requesting a pause and hearing blame. Agree a workable arrangement, then each try a short role; record rotation or pausing honestly.

steps.title: Read the full story without unsafe imitation
steps.text: The deer-and-monkey story spans six panels on pages 30–32, from difficulties through different helpful abilities to each receiving wanted food. Read or hear all six and identify both contributions. Animal actions are not instructions for children to cross rivers, climb or eat leaves.
steps.activity: Actually read or hear all six panels, use panel numbers to describe a change and each contribution, with tabletop role cards only. No river, climbing, carrying or tasting. Review actual site cooperation, express one real help and one unfinished item, and keep future plans separate.

manual: Actually perform both visible target-card trials: independently read and place once, then hear and confirm the helper’s stated target before placing. Compare communication, with no blindfold or claim of completed textbook nose play or guaranteed speed.
With agreement, actually sort six cards into two groups of three, one sorting and one checking, then exchange roles and repeat. Record both contributions without claiming school cleaning.
Actually play two tabletop pointing turns each and hear responses. Discussion or merely standing together is not actual coordinated play.
Actually use two familiar lawful lines; both try, agree prompts and each check a line. Name specific help, with no racing, guaranteed speed or forced memorisation.

Actually read or hear all four page-32 role-disagreement scenes, then rehearse the original responses to the same desired role, refusal of another role, a pause and blame. Leave missing source material pending.

Actually state both wishes and agree roles before trying a short introduction and pointing. Record rotation or pause; no confirmation without consent, coercion or claiming real-classmate activity with an adult.

Actually read or hear all six deer-and-monkey panels, describe a numbered change and both contributions, then review actual help and unfinished items. No river, climbing, carrying or tasting; plans stay separate.

pairs.material: Fictional tabletop trials: in A, the child sees the specified circle and places independently. In B, an adult names the square and the child confirms and places. Both can see; no timing data exist.
pairs.prompt: Which trial reads the target independently?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which trial has explicit prompting and confirmation?
pairs.explanation: Both solo and prompted processes can be described; no timing data means no speed conclusion.

pairs.material: Fictional tidying: Ning and an adult agree sorting and checking roles and both actually contribute. An only plans to tidy together later.
pairs.prompt: Who has actual divided-work cooperation?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only has a future cooperation plan?
pairs.explanation: Agreement and actual contributions differ from a plan.

pairs.material: Fictional roles: He wants to introduce, hears the other person and agrees to rotation. Zhu asks to pause and hears agreement to rest.
pairs.prompt: Who negotiates rotation of the same role?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who expresses a pause and hears a response?
pairs.explanation: Rotation and pausing are different communication results. A pause or declining a role is not a moral fault.

pairs.material: Six-panel source-story card: the deer helps the monkey across the river. The monkey uses climbing ability to obtain peaches and help the deer obtain leaves. Discuss only, without imitating unsafe actions.
pairs.prompt: Which story character helps the other reach the opposite bank?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which uses climbing ability to help obtain food?
pairs.explanation: The characters contribute different abilities. These animal actions are not instructions for children.

reflections: What actually happened in dividing work, prompting, shared reading or role communication? What helped or still needs adjustment? Pausing and discomfort may be expressed without grading feelings.
How might you divide work or communicate next time? Separate agreement, actual actions and future wishes. Do not state that cooperation always improves speed or happiness.

lesson9.title: This is my family
lesson9.goal: Identify stated family relationships, hear stories and observe similarities and differences; discuss the full interaction story without guessing ancestry or demanding disclosure.
lesson9.prerequisite: An adult may read. Fictional family cards can replace personal disclosure; photos and real names are unnecessary.
lesson9.parentTip: The textbook depicts one family arrangement, not a requirement for every family, household or ancestry. Respect differing caregivers and arrangements. Similar looks, interests or habits prove no relationship, and habits are not fixed at birth. Identify only stated relationships; no invented blanks, names, addresses, photos or secrets. Occupation and wealth do not rank families. Feelings may remain private; no forced immediate reconciliation. Seek a trusted adult for worry or harm.

steps.title: A birth story needs a stated source
steps.text: Page 34 has adult-told early-life stories. Something not personally remembered can be labelled as heard from someone. Families differ and the source or fictional story may be used instead of private experience.
steps.activity: Actually read or hear the page-34 birth story and identify it as a textbook character’s experience. If willing, ask a caregiver one shareable early-life question and hear a response. Label source discussion versus real inquiry; no names, photos or addresses.

steps.title: Relationship cards and each person’s importance
steps.text: Page 35 explicitly labels father, mother, paternal grandmother, maternal grandfather and the narrator. Other blanks cannot establish age or gender by position. Our fictional cards explicitly define paternal grandparents as father’s parents and maternal grandparents as mother’s parents; older/younger brother or sister refers to a male/female child with the same parents and the stated relative age in this example only.
steps.activity: Actually draw or place eleven original cards: narrator, father, mother, four grandparents and older/younger brother/sister. Explain every card from its stated relationship; ask rather than guess source blanks. Fictional cards suffice without a real family tree upload.

steps.title: Similarities do not prove family ties
steps.text: Page 36 discusses work habits, interests and physical resemblance. Similarities and differences can be observed without assuming ancestry fixes habits or that different looks negate family. No names, photos or private features are needed.
steps.activity: Use original preferences: A and a caregiver both like reading; B likes folding while a caregiver likes reading. Actually name one stated similarity and one difference. A voluntary non-private example or fictional discussion is enough; no genetic conclusion.

steps.title: Hear family stories and respond honestly
steps.text: Page 37 introduces relatives’ work and skills. Respect different work and care without occupational ranking. Label heard information; the source soldier and teacher are not facts about the learner’s family. Original fictional event: He and a caregiver put away two scattered books, check them and He says thanks. Discuss only, without climbing to find books.
steps.activity: Actually read or hear all three page-37 introductions and identify them as source examples. Then hear one freely shareable small event or our fictional book-organising story and respond, naming its source. No inquiry about occupation, workplace or address is required.

steps.title: Eight sibling panels and different feelings
steps.text: Eight panels across pages 34–37 include birth, joint activities, conflict and reconciliation, resemblance and difference, small shared secrets and wishes. Read all eight without requiring a real younger sister or instant reconciliation. Private secrets need not be disclosed; worry or harm can be told to a trusted adult.
steps.activity: Actually read or hear all eight panels and describe a numbered change, similarity or difference, and wishes versus occurred events. Separately rehearse a fictional card character’s request for turns or a pause and hear a response. Source, role-play and real experience stay distinct.

manual: Actually read or hear the source birth story and label it as a book example. Any voluntary real inquiry is separately sourced, with no invented birth memories, photos or addresses.
Actually read or place all eleven fictional relationship cards and explain every explicitly stated relation. Do not guess unlabeled source blanks or require a real family to match the example.
Actually name one stated preference similarity and one difference. Do not infer ancestry from appearance or fixed inheritance from habits; fictional examples suffice.

Actually read or hear all three page-37 introductions, then hear a freely shareable small event or the fictional book-organising story, label its source and respond. No workplace, occupation, income or address inquiry.

Actually read or hear all eight sibling panels and use numbers to describe a change, similarity or difference and wishes versus events. Missing material stays pending; having no siblings is not failure.
Actually rehearse a fictional card character expressing a wish for turns or a pause and hear a response. No forced real reconciliation, shared secrets or physical contact.

Actually review the site activity records and express one discussion, role-play or voluntary event and one unknown, then hear a response. Different families and feelings are not graded; plans remain separate.

pairs.material: Original fictional relationship cards: a paternal grandmother is father’s mother; a maternal grandfather is mother’s father. No appearance or diagram-position guesses.
pairs.prompt: Which is father’s mother?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which is mother’s father?
pairs.explanation: Use stated relationships without requiring every real family to match or live together.

pairs.material: Fictional preferences: A and a caregiver both like reading. B likes folding and a caregiver likes reading. Only preferences are stated, not ancestry.
pairs.prompt: Which card states shared reading interest?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which states differing interests?
pairs.explanation: Interests prove or disprove no family ties or fixed inheritance.

pairs.material: Fictional story records: He actually hears an adult’s past book-organising event and labels the source. Zhu only plans to ask tomorrow.
pairs.prompt: Who has an occurred story and source record?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only records a future inquiry?
pairs.explanation: Heard experiences need sources; plans are not events or personal memories.

pairs.material: Original fictional sibling cards explicitly identify an older brother and a younger sister relative to the narrator. They state no real family membership.
pairs.prompt: Who is stated to be older than the narrator?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who is stated to be younger?
pairs.explanation: Use stated identity and age relations; do not guess blanks or require real siblings.

reflections: What did you actually do when hearing a story, discussing cards or role-playing? What remains unknown? Fictional discussion is enough, without family secrets or rankings.
How might you hear stories or express needs next time? Separate imagination and hopes from occurred events; no demand for immediate acceptance or reconciliation.

lesson10.title: Caring for one another in a family
lesson10.goal: Read different forms of care, separate stories from real experiences, and practise asking before showing care while respecting family differences, privacy and needs.
lesson10.prerequisite: An adult may read the book. Fictional materials are enough; no photos, real birthdays, workplaces or private family experiences are required.
lesson10.parentTip: Families, living arrangements and caregivers differ. Do not rank care by money, gifts, jobs, contact or obedience. Uncomfortable touch can be declined and help can be needed; difficulty carrying a bag does not grade character. Adults handle illness: no medicines, lifting people or treatment. Birthdays may be unknown or private; use fictional dates. No names, addresses, photos or secrets are collected. Worry or harm can be shared with a trusted adult; do not require endurance or immediate reconciliation.

steps.title: Notice care without requiring one feeling
steps.text: Three children on page 38 describe different signs of care. Describe specific actions without guessing real family identities or requiring the same experience. Fictional story: a caregiver asks Xiaohe whether help putting away a book is wanted; Xiaohe agrees and the caregiver puts away one book. This is discussion material.
steps.activity: Read or hear all three textbook examples and the complete fictional story; identify request, consent and action. Optionally share a non-private small event, or use fiction only. No names or photos and no requirement to feel happy.

steps.title: Mutual care without ranking work
steps.text: Page 39 has two work pictures and three family-care pictures involving work, company, a gift and illness. Respect different work and caregiving; jobs and gifts do not measure love. A picture of care for illness is not a child treatment task.
steps.activity: Read or hear both work pictures and all three care pictures, distinguishing visible actions from unknown conditions. Discuss a fictional child asking whether quiet is wanted while adults care for illness and hearing a reply. Words only: no medicine, hot drinks or contact with an ill person.

steps.title: The complete four-picture schoolbag story
steps.text: The four bottom pictures across pages 38–39 discuss carrying a bag and independence. Read the request and response in sequence. Try suitable tasks, but explain weight, discomfort or support needs. Not doing one task for a child does not by itself establish a lack of care.
steps.activity: Read or hear all four pictures and describe the question, response and unspecified conditions by number. With desk cards, rehearse saying you can place a card yourself and saying you need help, hearing responses. No heavy bags or removing assistive items.

steps.title: Three care situations and birthday cards
steps.text: The three pictures on page 40 concern busy family members, company and leaving home; four birthday entries follow. Ask before offering care, rather than assuming loneliness or requiring hugs. Unknown birthdays can stay unknown; real dates are not needed here.
steps.activity: Discuss the three pictures and rehearse asking a busy adult whether they want to hear one sentence, asking a resting character whether company is wanted, and expressing a leaving-home message under caregiver arrangements. Fictional cards: A March 2, B May 6, C unknown, D chooses privacy. Distinguish all four without guessing.
