steps.title: A small action with consent and honest review
steps.text: Care may be words, listening or a suitable action, while respecting refusal and pause. Plans, agreement and completed actions are separate. Do not require identical responses or immediate real-family reconciliation.
steps.activity: Ask whether a person wants one desk paper card; do it only after consent and hear the reply. Alternatively use fictional-role rehearsal and label it. Review actual actions, refusal/pause and pending items; keep future care plans separate and family matters private.

manual: Read or hear all three page-38 care examples and the complete fictional one-book story; identify request, consent and action. Fiction is enough, with no names, photos or forced happiness.
Read or hear both page-39 work pictures and all three care pictures, naming actions and unknown conditions. Do not rank jobs or gifts; illness is discussion only, with no medicine or hot drinks.
Read or hear all four schoolbag-story pictures and identify requests and responses by number; rehearse placing a desk card and asking for help. No heavy bags or character judgments about help.
Discuss all three page-40 busy, company and leaving-home pictures; ask whether care is wanted and listen. Do not assume being alone means loneliness or go out alone.
Read all four fictional birthday cards: A March 2, B May 6, C unknown, D private. Distinguish given dates, unknowns and privacy; do not give real birthdays or guess book blanks.
Actually rehearse three fictional communications: asking a busy person, offering company and a leaving-home message. Hear responses and allow pause or refusal; no required hugs or doing adult work.

With consent actually carry out a safe desk care action and hear a response, or clearly label fictional rehearsal. Review actual, refused/paused and pending actions; future plans do not prove family improvement.

pairs.material: Fictional care records: A asks to pass a paper card and does so after consent; B asks, hears that it is not needed and pauses.
pairs.prompt: Which passed a card after consent?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which respected the reply by pausing?
pairs.explanation: Listen to agreement and refusal. Pausing does not mean a lack of care.

pairs.material: Fictional birthday cards: A explicitly says March 2; B says the date is unknown with no other clues.
pairs.prompt: Which gives an explicit date?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which must remain unknown?
pairs.explanation: Do not guess unknown dates or require real birthdays.

pairs.material: Fictional desk records: Xiaohe says they can place a card and does so with consent; Xiaozhu asks for help and the adult agrees to help.
pairs.prompt: Who has already placed the card?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who explained a help need and heard agreement?
pairs.explanation: Abilities differ. Agreement to help is not completion, and help does not negate care.

pairs.material: Fictional records: Xiaoning completed a request-and-listening role-play with an adult; Xiaoan only wrote a future request plan.
pairs.prompt: Who records actual role-play?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who only has a future plan?
pairs.explanation: Role-play, real-family experiences and plans are separate; do not claim relationships improved.

reflections: What did you actually read, ask, hear or rehearse, and which response needs respect? You need not discuss real family matters; refusal, pause and feelings are not graded.
How might you show care next time? Separate hopes, consent and events, without requiring immediate acceptance or reconciliation.

lesson11.title: Let me help put things away
lesson11.goal: Recognise uses, discuss scattered belongings, and actually sort, label, retrieve, use and return items with suitable help; keep future plans separate.
lesson11.prerequisite: An adult may read. Ordinary paper cards and safe desk space are enough; no storage purchases or room photos are required.
lesson11.parentTip: Participation does not mean having to do everything independently. Ask for help or use accessible methods; room size, possessions, speed and difficulty are not scored. Handle only willing personal items an adult confirms safe: no scissors, medicines, electrical equipment or cleaning chemicals, climbing or heavy lifting. Do not dispose of others’ things. Sock and shoe examples do not require identical use or diagnose abilities. Adults follow item-specific care instructions, rather than washing everything.

steps.title: Belongings and two riddles
steps.text: Page 41 shows toys and school materials with two riddles for socks and shoes. Items can support activities; how many someone owns does not grade them. Riddle imagery does not require identical clothing or bodily experiences.
steps.activity: Read or hear the examples and both riddles, identify socks and shoes from clues and describe one use in your own words. Alternatively use book, paper-and-pencil, toy, sock, shoe and ball cards. No sharp tools or private possessions are needed.

steps.title: Two scattered-item situations; do not guess causes
steps.text: The two page-42 pictures concern finding an eraser and an adult tidying again. Scattered items can make finding or passage harder, but pictures do not prove deliberate loss or describe a real home. Help finding things can be requested.
steps.activity: Read or hear both and distinguish visible situations from unknown causes. Discuss desk records: a book card in the play area and a ball card in the study area. Identify mismatches with the agreed rule, without actually losing objects or creating trip hazards.

steps.title: Sort, label and retrieve separately
steps.text: Page 43 shows sorting, arranging, labels and suitable places. Agree categories by use; labels match areas. Actually test retrieval after placing, rather than treating a label as completed tidying.
steps.activity: Sort six cards under explicit uses: book/paper-and-pencil for study, toy/ball for play, socks/shoes for wearing. Arrange three area labels and the matching cards. On hearing “book card in study”, retrieve and return it. Symbols can replace writing; no real scissors.

steps.title: Use and return; suitable care differs
steps.text: The page-43 verse also concerns returning and caring for objects. Care methods differ, so not everything goes in water. Adults use item instructions and conditions; this site discusses rather than applying chemicals or handling electronics.
steps.activity: Actually take a willing card from its labelled place, view it once and return it, checking the label. Separately discuss keeping ordinary paper dry and following adult instructions for an item confirmed washable. No actual washing. Record taking, using, returning and discussion separately.

steps.title: Agreed timing and a small contribution
steps.text: Page 44 shows scheduled tidying and returning to place, plus statements about postponing participation and expecting another to do it. Contribute what is suitable with help; support needs are not avoidance. A future agreed time is not completed action.
steps.activity: Read or hear both methods and both statements, then agree a feasible tidying time. If now is agreed, actually tidy one safe desk area and review. If later, leave it pending until the real time arrives. Record personal contribution, help and future plans without declaring a lasting habit.

manual: Read or hear page-41 examples and both riddles; use clues to identify socks and shoes and describe uses. Cards are enough; identical possessions or bodily experiences are not required.
Read or hear both page-42 pictures, discussing effects and unknown causes; identify the fictional book/ball area mismatches. No actual losses or assumptions of deliberate difficulty.
Actually sort six use cards into study (book/paper-and-pencil), play (toy/ball) and wearing (socks/shoes), explaining the rule. Discussion does not prove a real room was tidied.
Actually arrange three area labels and cards, then retrieve and return the specified book card from study. Check labels, placement and retrieval separately; accessible symbols are allowed.
Actually take a willing ordinary card, view it and return it to its original place, checking the location. Using and returning are separate actions, not confirmed by quiz answers.
Actually discuss keeping paper dry and adult/item instructions for something washable. No immersion of arbitrary items, chemicals or electronics; this is discussion, not washing.
Read or hear both page-44 methods and both postponement/delegation statements, agreeing participation and help suited to ability. Agreement is not execution; help is not graded.

At the agreed real time, actually tidy one safe desk area and review contribution and assistance. Future time stays pending; no climbing, heavy lifting or disposing of others’ things. Keep future plans separate.

pairs.material: Explicit fictional use cards: A is book and paper-and-pencil cards for study; B is toy and ball cards for play. No real sharp objects are involved.
pairs.prompt: Which follows a study-use rule?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which follows a play-use rule?
pairs.explanation: Use the explicit rule. Other reasonable real-life rules can exist; categories do not grade children or items.

pairs.material: Fictional records: A only plans to label later; B placed a study label and book card, then actually retrieved and returned it.
pairs.prompt: Which only has a labelling plan?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which records labels, placement and retrieval?
pairs.explanation: Plans, labels and retrieval are separate. Ideas do not automatically confirm tidying.

pairs.material: Care cards: A is ordinary paper to keep dry; B is an item an adult has confirmed washable under its instructions, with the method arranged by that adult.
pairs.prompt: Which should stay dry?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which still follows adult and item instructions for washing?
pairs.explanation: Do not immerse arbitrary items. Discussion only: no chemicals or electronics handled by children.

pairs.material: Fictional records: Xiaoning tidied a desk area at the agreed real time and recorded help; Xiaoan agreed tomorrow, which has not arrived.
pairs.prompt: Who records actual tidying?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who should keep the activity pending?
pairs.explanation: Help may be recorded without being avoidance. Future times do not prove completion or habits.

reflections: Which cards did you actually sort, place, retrieve or return, and where do you need help? No room photos or private information; difficulties and accessible methods are ungraded.
When and which small part might you tidy next? Separate agreement, execution and future plans; one attempt is not a lasting habit.

lesson12.title: Learning to help with housework
lesson12.goal: Recognise contributions, actually learn folding and a suitable new method, discuss abilities and help, and record real participation and seven-day reminders without automatic completion.
lesson12.prerequisite: An adult may read and provide willing clean shirt/shorts and a safe desk. Missing materials leave that practical task pending; paper answers do not replace folding.
lesson12.parentTip: Participate under caregiver checks and abilities, with help and pauses; no scores by gender, speed, home circumstances or difficulties. Sweeping, rubbish and dishes are picture discussions: no unknown rubbish, sharp broken things, hot water, chemicals, electrical equipment or collecting deliveries alone. Fold ordinary safe clothing without climbing or heavy lifting. Shoelaces use an adult-checked desk shoe and known method, never around the body; learning is not guaranteed for everyone. Label paper substitutes without claiming real folding or all pictured chores. Future dates stay pending.

steps.title: The housework tree: five examples and a blank
steps.text: Five pictured apples on page 45 concern sweeping, wiping, rubbish, books and tableware, with one blank. Picture counts are not ability rankings or completed chores.
steps.activity: Read or hear all five and discuss whose checks and help are needed. Optionally name a safe past contribution or something to learn, separating done from planned. Do not guess a fixed blank answer or use dangerous rubbish or knives.

steps.title: Three experiences; contributions and feelings differ
steps.text: The three page-46 experiences concern sharing work, sweeping difficulty and first-time dishes. Suitable participation can practise skills, without guaranteed happiness or quick mastery. Explain difficulty rather than deliberately making wet clothes.
steps.activity: Read or hear all three, distinguishing contribution, difficulty and unknown conditions. Rehearse willing card placement, requesting a demonstration and asking to pause, each with a response. No real rubbish, dishes or deliberate wet clothing.

steps.title: Two garments: read six pictures, then fold
steps.text: The shirt and shorts on page 47 each have three stages from spreading to aligning and folding smaller. In this site’s own words: lay a shirt flat, bring sleeves inward and fold top to bottom; lay shorts flat, align the legs and fold smaller. Ask for a demonstration suited to the actual garment.
steps.activity: Read or hear all six pictures, then actually fold a willing clean shirt and shorts separately on an adult-checked desk, spreading, aligning, folding and reviewing. Record help; no size conformity or races. Leave a missing garment pending; cards do not prove real folding.

steps.title: Another method and three conversations
steps.text: Page 47 also shows learning shoelaces and introducing a method; page 48 has adults declining help, strength limitations and a request during reading. Safety, willingness and timing can be discussed. Help or declining a movement is not laziness; deliveries do not become a child’s solo stranger-contact task.
steps.activity: An adult demonstrates a known lace method with an existing safe shoe on a desk. The child watches, attempts feasible steps and explains difficulty without body loops or guaranteed mastery. With card roles, rehearse hearing help is not wanted, changing a too-heavy task and negotiating time during reading. No real mopping or delivery collection.

steps.title: Seven-day reminders and one actual contribution
steps.text: The seven-day table on page 48 has some ticks; blanks do not automatically mean completion or failure. Reminders, future dates and actions differ. Do not invent a whole week before it occurs.
steps.activity: Draw seven Monday–Sunday cells and choose an adult-approved project and feasible time. Review folding already done here or participate in suitable desk housework, recording the child’s contribution, help and actual date. Future cells stay pending and unknowns stay unknown. Explain one possible adjustment; future plans are separate, without extra repeated burden.

manual: Read or hear all five pictured page-45 apples and the blank; discuss checks and help for sweeping, wiping, rubbish, books and tableware. Optionally name done/planned work without guessing a fixed blank or ranking quantities.

Read or hear all three page-46 experiences, separating contribution, difficulty and feeling; rehearse participation, demonstration and pause requests with responses. No deliberate wet clothes or dangerous rubbish.
Read or hear all six page-47 shirt/shorts pictures, three each, describing spreading, alignment and folding. Reading does not claim actual folding.

After adult checks, actually fold a willing clean shirt by spreading, bringing sleeves inward and folding, then review. Adjust with demonstration, label help, leave missing materials pending and avoid races.

After adult checks, actually fold willing clean shorts by spreading, aligning legs and folding, then review. Missing materials stay separately pending; cards do not replace real completion or require a uniform size.

Actually watch a known adult lace method on a safe desk shoe, attempt feasible steps and describe difficulty, or demonstrate a method you really know for a partner to try. Missing conditions stay pending; no body loops or guaranteed learning.

Read or hear all three page-48 situations and rehearse card-role requests/responses for unwanted help, strength limits and reading-time negotiation. No forced uncomfortable actions or solo delivery pickup.

Actually draw seven Monday–Sunday reminder cells with suitable project/time, separating happened, future-pending and unknown entries. Do not copy book ticks as facts or score future/blank cells as failures.

Actually review one completed folding task or adult-approved safe chore with date, contribution, help and a possible adjustment. Unhappened stays pending; no repeated burden or invented seven days, and future plans separate.

pairs.material: Fictional records: A actually folded a clean shirt and recorded help; B only viewed its three pictures and has not folded.
pairs.prompt: Which records actual folding?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which only records picture reading?
pairs.explanation: Reading and doing differ. Help does not erase contribution; answers cannot confirm chores.

pairs.material: Fictional communication: Xiaohe requests a demonstration and hears a response; Xiaozhu explains current reading and agrees to place cards later.
pairs.prompt: Who requests method support?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Who negotiates participation time?
pairs.explanation: Help and timing differ. An agreement is not action, and help is not laziness.

pairs.material: Explicit reminder cells: A is today with shorts actually folded and dated; B is tomorrow, not yet arrived or done.
pairs.prompt: Which can record a completed event?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which stays future-pending?
pairs.explanation: Do not invent ticks or grade future/unknown cells as failures; no lasting-habit claim.

pairs.material: Fictional materials: A is adult-checked clean ordinary clothing willingly folded at a desk; B is unknown rubbish potentially containing broken sharp objects, not handled here.
pairs.prompt: Which permits folding under checked conditions?
pairs.reviewPrompt: Which should not be handled by the child here?
pairs.explanation: Check each condition rather than assuming every chore is suitable or involving dangerous things.

reflections: What did you actually learn, fold or discuss, who helped, and what remains pending? Record difficulties and feelings honestly without photos or private home information.
Which small contribution might you try and when do you need a demonstration? Separate reminders, agreement, real dates and plans; a table does not prove seven completed days.

lesson13.title: A happy Children’s Day
lesson13.goal: Learn about June 1, read celebrations and care examples, prepare and voluntarily share an activity, and discuss children’s rights and needs. Separate actual, simulated and future events.
lesson13.prerequisite: Ordinary paper and a pen suffice. An adult may read. Existing lawful song material can help; no gifts, donations, martial arts or large gathering are required.
lesson13.parentTip: Respect the child’s wishes and an adult-approved setting. Watching, pointing, assistance, pausing and different feelings are allowed. Book events and historical photos do not prove today’s date, school arrangements or membership. Do not upload identities or medical details, copy medical procedures or use unsafe stages. Book giving is voluntary and adult-managed, with channels checked. Rights are not earned through grades, donations or obedience.

steps.title: The full celebration spread: preparation and performance
steps.text: Pages 50–51 show singing Tongxin Xiang Dang (童心向党), fan crafts, choosing and preparing an activity, dance, martial arts and an audience. The book’s first Children’s Day after school entry is not proof that today or our school has the same event; scarves do not determine a learner’s membership.
steps.activity: Read all six categories. With existing lawful material, listen to an adult demonstrate the named song and optionally try a line; record listening and trying separately. This site does not reproduce lyrics or audio. Discuss dance and martial arts without requiring imitation or a stage.

steps.title: Choice, consent and actual preparation
steps.text: Choosing, preparing and already presenting are different. In an original tabletop sharing, choose a short original introduction, an existing lawful song or explaining a paper fan; being an audience member is allowed. A home activity is not a whole-school event.
steps.activity: Discuss roles, materials and how to pause, hearing both wishes. Fold ordinary paper alternately back and forth, then hold one end to form a fan, without scissors, staples or glue. Record help; missing materials remain unfinished. Prepare the chosen content; unagreed roles remain unagreed.

steps.title: Actual participation and four experiences
steps.text: Page 52 shows play with a partner, a family performance, a community celebration and choosing books for children in mountain areas. Experiences and feelings differ; neither gifts nor donation rank a child, and recipients are not all alike.
steps.activity: In an adult-approved tabletop space, actually show the fan or chosen introduction, hear a response and swap sharing/audience roles once. Label a simulation honestly. Read all four experiences; share one real remembered occasion or keep it unknown. Wishes are separate.

steps.title: Voluntary care is not a completed donation
steps.text: Choosing books and the next-page donation are care examples. A proposal, owner consent, a checked channel and actual delivery are different. Care is not limited to spending or donating; respect opinions, privacy and different resources.
steps.activity: Discuss fictional book cards A and B separately: A has owner consent but an unchecked channel; B lacks owner consent. Explain the missing conditions and role-play asking and hearing a response. Do not mail, pay, message or reveal recipients. Card discussion is not an actual donation.

steps.title: Three care examples and children’s rights
steps.text: Page 53 shows textbook historical examples of Xi Jinping at a Children’s Day event, a doctors’ free clinic and book donors. Do not invent a year or location. June 1 is celebrated as Children’s Day in China. Children have rights to life, development, protection and participation, with learning, rest and opportunities to express views; these do not depend on a good performance or a donation.
steps.activity: Read all three examples and captions. In original fictional situations, role-play asking a trusted adult for care when unwell, for rest and to hear an activity suggestion; listen to a response in each. No medical imitation or forced disclosure. Review actual participation, preparation, reading and unfinished work separately from future plans.

manual: Read all six spread categories: song, fan, choice/preparation, dance, martial arts and audience. Do not infer today, school events or membership.

Using existing lawful material, actually hear Tongxin Xiang Dang (童心向党) and optionally try a line. Record each separately; missing material stays unfinished. An original introduction does not replace learning the named song.
Actually discuss content, roles, materials and pausing, hearing both wishes. Unagreed roles stay unfinished; no forced performance or happiness.
Actually fold ordinary paper back and forth and hold one end to make a fan; prepare the chosen sharing. Record adult assistance, use no scissors or staples, and keep missing materials unfinished.

Actually show the fan or chosen introduction in an approved place, hear a response and swap sharing/audience roles once. Label a simulation; do not claim a school celebration or martial-arts performance.
Read all four partner/family/community/book-giving examples. Share one real holiday memory or keep it unknown; wishes are separate and feelings ungraded.
Discuss both fictional book cards, distinguishing owner consent and an unchecked channel. Practice asking and hearing wishes; no mailing, payments or messaging, and no actual donation claim.

Read the rights explanation and separately role-play care, rest and an opportunity to suggest something, hearing adult responses. Rights are not traded for grades, performances or gifts; no forced medical disclosure.

lesson14.title: The Young Pioneers
lesson14.goal: Read activity and history examples, learn the organization’s name and membership conditions, learn scarf, song and salute separately, and attempt an appropriate service. Distinguish wishes, preparation and formal status.
lesson14.prerequisite: An adult may read the book and official material. Ordinary paper supports original crafting. Scarf and song practice require adult-approved suitable materials and lawful demonstration; missing material stays unfinished.
lesson14.parentTip: Separate the 2025 constitution from historical examples. Formal status is established by the organization, never clothing, age or website completion. Wishes, application, requirements and approval differ. School organizations handle actual admission and ceremonies; this site does not apply, message or grant membership. No reproduced lyrics/audio. Do not play with, tug or tightly bind a scarf or use a rope around the neck; adult supervision is required. Assistance, pausing and different feelings are allowed, without ranking physical ability. Keep unknown school arrangements unknown.

steps.title: Three examples and your own feelings
steps.text: Page 54 shows school-gate service, a tree-planting activity and hearing/singing the team song. These illustrate members’ activities, not the learner’s status or an instruction to stand at a gate or plant independently. Feelings can differ.
steps.activity: Read all three, naming the activity and who it may help. Share a feeling or a question without requiring excitement. Do not perform gate duty, dig or invent school arrangements.

steps.title: The name and three materials from different periods
steps.text: The full name is 中国少年先锋队, the Young Pioneers of China. Page 55 discusses the Anyuan Children’s Corps as a predecessor, a Chuangzao Cup innovation activity and contemporary aspirations. Historical pictures do not establish today’s events or school participation.
steps.activity: Read the name and all three materials, separating earlier history, innovation and aspirations without invented dates. Make an original paper item, explain its purpose, change something and try it, such as a folded holder for a large paper card. This is not competition participation, a patent or an official team activity.

steps.title: Wishing, preparing and formal confirmation
steps.text: Page 56 introduces preparation. The 2025 constitution sets ages 6–14, willingness to join and follow the constitution, application to the school organization, meeting requirements and approval before membership. Age, learning or wearing a scarf alone does not grant status.
steps.activity: Read the sequence. Compare fictional A still learning requirements with B explicitly approved as a member. Express wishes and questions and draw an anonymous preparation list. Do not submit it as a real application; families can ask schools about actual arrangements.

steps.title: Three preparations, each separately
steps.text: Page 56 has learning the scarf, team song and salute. The song is 我们是共产主义接班人, with words by Zhou Yuhui and music by Ji Ming. The salute uses the right hand with fingers together raised above the head, expressing priority for the people’s interests. Learning is not a formal ceremony.
steps.activity: An adult checks official guidance and demonstrates four steps from the wearer’s perspective: drape over the shoulders with the wide point at the centre of the back and the right end below the left at the crossing; bring the right end in front of the left and across to the right; bring it through the crossing gap to make one loop around the left; pass the right end through that loop and arrange the knot. With suitable materials, willingness and direct supervision, practice the appropriate drape and tie without neck pressure or active play; paper observation is not wearing. With lawful material, hear the complete song and optionally sing along; no lyrics/audio here. An adult demonstrates the right hand’s five fingers together, raised past the chest about a fist above the head, palm toward the front-left/down, then supports a voluntary attempt. Record observation, assistance or pausing honestly.

steps.title: Further preparation: a real small service
steps.text: Learning requirements, studying and appropriately helping others are forms of preparation. A helpful act does not automatically grant membership. Record real contributions, help and unfinished work separately from wishes and school approval.
steps.activity: Propose one safe approved service, such as returning usable shared-reading books after hearing someone’s needs and agreeing. Actually do it and label adult help. Review reading, crafting and each of the three preparations separately; missing song or scarf materials remain unfinished. Keep future questions separate, without messaging an application or approving membership.

No neck pressure, tugging or rope loops; missing material stays unfinished and paper observation is not wearing.

Actually perform one approved appropriate service and review contributions, help and unfinished preparations. Label adult participation; formal status and future arrangements remain separate without school approval by this site.

lesson15.title: Wearing the red scarf
lesson15.goal: Recognise ceremonies, flags and the red scarf; read the four care panels and four growth activities. Actual care requires materials; formal membership and personal learning remain separate.
lesson15.prerequisite: An adult can read the book and official guidance. A missing scarf does not prevent learning; wearing or washing remains pending until suitable materials and guidance are available.
lesson15.parentTip: Do not infer membership from age or clothing, or grant membership or awards through the website. Formal ceremonies follow the school organisation. Feelings and assisted participation are not graded. Never pull or tighten around the neck or require a purchase. Confirm fabric and safe care before washing; no unknown cleaners or personal identity collection.

steps.title: Four ceremony pictures and personal experience
steps.text: Page 57 shows scarf presentation, the oath, the call and a first salute. The oath and call use a fist; the salute raises the joined fingers of the right hand above the head. Roles and actions differ.
steps.activity: Actually read all four and identify the activities. Describe an induction only if actually attended; not yet a member or unknown is acceptable. Web practice is not a formal ceremony; membership is handled by the school organisation under the charter.

steps.title: The Party flag and two team flags
steps.text: Page 58 shows the Party flag with its emblem, a rectangular brigade flag and a detachment flag with a swallowtail cut. Both team flags show a star and torch: Party leadership, light and revolutionary victory are the respective meanings of star, torch and red.
steps.activity: Read all three flags, names, visible distinctions and team-flag meanings. Do not confuse them with the national flag, manufacture symbols or invent dimensions. Mention a previous sighting only if actually remembered; otherwise say unknown.

steps.title: Scarf meaning and use
steps.text: The red scarf marks Young Pioneer membership and symbolises a corner of the red flag; the reference to martyrs’ blood is symbolic, not physical contact. Follow organisational arrangements for team events and important ceremonies. It may be omitted during sports, work or home rest; in heat, the official guidance uses a badge.
steps.activity: Read the meaning and use situations with an adult. Ask the school organisation about its actual requirements. Missing materials or unknown membership must not become a claim of wearing. Constant forced wear is not care, and personal feelings are not ranked.

steps.title: Yueyue’s four care panels
steps.text: The lower story across pages 57–58 has four panels only: an adult reminder, neat wearing before school, folding after returning home and washing when dirty. Care requires suitable actions, rather than wearing constantly.
steps.activity: Read and retell all four. With suitable materials and adult guidance, wear, remove, lay flat and fold neatly; left and right refer to the wearer. Ask the counsellor to demonstrate unfamiliar steps and never pull the neck. Separately wash and dry only when needed and after confirming fabric and method; missing conditions remain pending. Ordinary paper is not a real scarf.

steps.title: Four growth activities and a real small contribution
steps.text: Page 59 shows a revolutionary martyrs’ memorial visit, team knowledge learning, a science exhibition and suitable helpful actions. Honesty, courage, liveliness and unity are the team’s style. These photos do not establish your participation.
steps.activity: Read all four. With an adult choose a lawful history or science introduction, actually read or listen to a part and state its source and a question. Missing material remains pending; home reading is not a site visit. After agreement, actually give safe help within your ability, such as arranging your own tabletop with a clean cloth. Record your contribution and keep future efforts separate from formal team events.

lesson16.title: Learn from role models and act
lesson16.goal: Read role-model material and discuss work, learning, perseverance, creativity, contribution and gratitude. Actually share and undertake suitable small actions; distinguish history, fictional rehearsal, national awards and personal learning.
lesson16.prerequisite: An adult can read the book and lawful role-model sources; use personal paper and books. An adult supplies sourced national youth stories; actual reading stays pending without material.
lesson16.parentTip: The website grants no role-model or national youth title and does not rank grades, disability or family income. Historical work or thrift does not require driving, collecting scrap, withholding food or water, excessive work or donations. Read a charity-sale picture only; no unapproved money collection. Read care scenes without feeding, medication or infection exposure. Thanks are voluntary and assistance can be stated.

steps.title: Lei Feng and two kinds of sharing
steps.text: Page 60 introduces Lei Feng and historical photos of sharing thrift with Young Pioneers and driving skills with fellow soldiers. These describe historical activities, not instructions for a child to drive or collect metal.
steps.activity: Read both photos and identify the shared content. This brief paraphrase uses Hunan Lei Feng Memorial Museum’s Thrift Box account: he retained reusable old parts, found suitable pieces when needed and returned surplus to the collective. An adult may add lawful original material. Learn to value safe existing belongings, not scrap collection, repair or withholding water.

steps.title: Tell a story actually read
steps.text: Admired people and feelings may differ. State whether a story comes from the book, lawful material or personal experience; an adult’s historical account is not your eyewitness experience.
steps.activity: Actually read or listen to the sourced short account above or a lawful story supplied by an adult, then retell the person, action, one possible lesson and source in your own words. Invent no details when material is missing; do not copy pages or recordings.

steps.title: Three sharing themes
steps.text: Page 61 suggests stories about enjoying work, perseverance and diligent learning. Original fictional cards: A arranges personal books by agreement; B asks an adult for help with an unfamiliar fold and tries again; C raises a question after reading and checks a source. These are fictional learning examples, not national award recipients.
steps.activity: Read all three themes and cards and discuss concrete actions. The 2026 national announcement has an explicit year, unlike the textbook’s undated classroom setting. An adult supplies a sourced national youth account for actual reading and discussion of theme and evidence; without it remain pending. Difficulty or help does not negate perseverance.

steps.title: Three qualities and nearby examples
steps.text: Page 62 illustrates model experiments, a charity sale and caring for a relative as creativity, contribution and gratitude. Pictures do not prove your participation in sales or feeding a patient; creativity can start with a safe small change.
steps.activity: Read all three and discuss suitable actions. steps.title: Small actions: contribution, thanks and plans
steps.text: Learning from a model does not immediately confer an award or adult responsibilities. Separate your contribution, a peer’s concrete action and future effort. No compelled private disclosure or physical contact.

Voluntarily express thanks through speech, a written card or assisted communication and record the response. Do not claim treatment or a real charity sale; future efforts are separate plans.
